subChunks.title: SLF4J, Log Levels & Structured Logging
subChunks.hookHtml: When your service fails at 3am, the only thing between you and a four-hour debugging session is your logs. Logging is the mechanism by which running software describes what it is doing. Getting it right is not an afterthought.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
SLF4J: The Logging Facade

SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is an abstraction layer — you write against the SLF4J API, and the actual implementation (Logback, Log4j2) is swapped in at runtime via the classpath. Spring Boot ships with Logback by default.

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public class SpellService {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(SpellService.class);

    public Spell getSpell(String id) {
        log.debug("Looking up spell: {}", id);
        // ...
        log.info("Spell retrieved: {} in {}ms", id, elapsed);
        return spell;
    }
}

The {} placeholder avoids string concatenation when the log level is disabled — the argument is only converted to a string if the level is active.

Log Levels (in ascending severity)

  • TRACE: Finest detail — method entry/exit, loop iterations. Disabled in production.
  • DEBUG: Developer diagnostics — intermediate values, query parameters. Off in production by default.
  • INFO: Normal operation milestones — service started, user logged in, job completed. Always on.
  • WARN: Unexpected but recoverable — missing optional config, retrying a failed call. Always on.
  • ERROR: A failure that needs attention — exception caught, payment failed, database unreachable. Always on.

What to Log and What Not to Log

Do log: application events (request received, job started), notable state changes, errors with context, slow operations.

Never log: passwords, credit card numbers, authentication tokens, PII (personal data such as full names and email addresses combined with sensitive context). Logging sensitive data creates a compliance and security breach.

Structured Logging

Add context using MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) — key-value pairs automatically included in every log line in the current thread:

import org.slf4j.MDC;

MDC.put("requestId", UUID.randomUUID().toString());
MDC.put("userId", user.getId());
try {
    log.info("Processing payment");
    // All logs in this thread include requestId and userId
} finally {
    MDC.clear();  // always clear to avoid leaking into subsequent requests
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's spell execution chamber runs thousands of castings a day. When one fails silently, the post-mortem team has only one tool: the logs. The lead investigator examines a log file and immediately finds the exact failure point, the user affected, and the time. Another team, whose service logged nothing useful, is still in the dark three hours later.

storyBeats.speaker: Lead Investigator Cass
storyBeats.text: Every Java professional uses SLF4J. You write to the Logger interface — never to System.out.println. The implementation (Logback in Spring Boot) decides the format, the destination, and which levels to show. In production you will typically see INFO and above.

storyBeats.speaker: Proper log level usage
storyBeats.text:
log.trace("Entering validate(), id={}", id);           // never in prod
log.debug("Query parameters: tier={}, minDamage={}", t, d); // dev only
log.info ("Spell {} retrieved in {}ms", name, elapsed);  // normal event
log.warn ("Spell service slow ({}ms > 500ms threshold)", t); // concerning
log.error("Failed to persist spell {}", id, exception);  // action needed

storyBeats.speaker: Lead Investigator Cass
storyBeats.text: The {} placeholder is not cosmetic. It delays string conversion until the level is actually enabled. If DEBUG is disabled in production and you write log.debug("Data: " + expensiveToString()), the toString() call happens even though the message is thrown away. Placeholders prevent this.

storyBeats.speaker: Lead Investigator Cass
storyBeats.text: MDC adds context that travels with the thread. Put a request ID in MDC at the start of every request. Every log line in that request's thread will carry it automatically. When you search logs for a specific request ID, you see its complete story from start to finish — even across multiple classes.

learningObjectives: Create an SLF4J Logger using LoggerFactory.getLogger() and write to all five levels
Explain what each log level represents and when to use it
Use {} placeholders instead of string concatenation for log messages
Use MDC to add correlated context to all log lines in a request
commonMistakes: Using System.out.println instead of a Logger — output is unstructured, has no level, and cannot be redirected
Logging sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII) — creates security and compliance exposure
String concatenation in log calls — the string is built even when the level is disabled
Forgetting MDC.clear() at the end of a request — context leaks into the next request on the same thread
assessmentCriteria: Can declare a Logger correctly (private static final, LoggerFactory.getLogger(ClassName.class))
Can assign the correct level to each scenario: service starting, unexpected null, payment failed, query params
Can explain why {} placeholders are more efficient than string concatenation in log calls
Can demonstrate MDC usage and explain why clear() must be in a finally block
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Java logging to a developer who has only used System.out.println. Why do we need a logging framework? What are the five log levels and when does each apply? What is MDC and why is it useful?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a SpellLogger class that demonstrates correct logging practice:

  1. Declare a static SLF4J Logger for the class
  2. Write a method void processSpell(String spellId, int damage) that logs: a DEBUG message with the spellId and damage, an INFO message saying the spell was processed, and if damage > 500, a WARN saying damage is exceptionally high
  3. Write a method void failedCast(String spellId, Exception e) that logs an ERROR with the spellId and exception
  4. In main, call both methods to demonstrate output
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch. Write a class RequestLogger that simulates request handling with MDC. The method void handleRequest(String requestId, String userId, String action) should: put requestId and userId into MDC, log INFO with the action, simulate a step that might fail (if action is "delete", log WARN), then clear MDC in a finally block. In main call it for two different requests and observe that each log line would carry the request context.

questions.questionHtml: Which log level should be used when a payment processing request fails with an unexpected exception?
questions.explanationHtml: ERROR is for failures that require attention — payment failures, database unreachable, unhandled exceptions. It indicates something went wrong that cannot be recovered from automatically and may need manual intervention.

options: The placeholder version is faster to type
The toString() call in the concatenation version happens regardless of whether DEBUG is enabled
Placeholder syntax supports more data types
String concatenation causes a compile error inside log calls
questions.correctAnswer: The toString() call in the concatenation version happens regardless of whether DEBUG is enabled
questions.explanationHtml: With string concatenation, expensiveObject.toString() and the concatenation both execute before the log method is even called — even if DEBUG is disabled and the message will be thrown away. Placeholders pass the object reference; SLF4J only calls toString() if the level is actually active.

questions.questionHtml: It is safe to log user passwords at DEBUG level because DEBUG is disabled in production.
questions.explanationHtml: Never log passwords, tokens, or sensitive PII at any level. Production debug logging is frequently enabled temporarily during incident response — and may remain enabled accidentally. Additionally, log files are often stored for months and may be accessible to multiple people. The rule is absolute: sensitive data never goes into logs.
